No one has habits, neither good nor bad. All habits are acquired or, rather,
developed. And if there is something that psychologists work on very frequently,
it is precisely habits. In fact, a large part of our work revolves around that,
helping others change their habits, abandon those that are not useful or constructive, and
replace them with better ones. And I tell you, it's not easy. If it were, if we could change them
easily, we would avoid many of the problems we have. Let's take a look.
In health sciences, and especially in psychology, we call a habit any behavior
that is repeated regularly. Habits, in themselves, are neither good nor bad; it depends
on which specific habit we are talking about to determine if it benefits us or
harms us. On one hand, we have what are known as 'bad habits,' which are the ones many
people spend half their lives trying to get rid of: drinking, smoking, or gambling,
to name three examples that are also considered addictions. But not all bad habits are
related to addictions; for example, speaking in a loud voice, being disrespectful,
driving recklessly, swearing, being late... all of these are also bad habits.
And of course, the other side of the coin is those habits that most of us want to develop
to contribute in various ways to improving our health or our lives:
exercise, healthy eating, reading, those related to
personal organization, order, cleanliness, etc. Therefore, we have both good habits and
bad habits depending on how they affect us. And how do we create habits? One of the
key elements for habit formation is repetition. The more we repeat a behavior,
the less effort it takes to carry it out, until we reach the point where
we develop it almost without thinking. This is great when it's a healthy habit, but when
it's a bad habit, it can pose quite a few difficulties when trying to get rid of it.
But, really, habits are not 'created'; we create them. It is us who
establish them based on our way of being and acting, and based on various influences:
our upbringing at home, at school, our values, our preferences, friendships,
our learning history... that's why different people have such diverse habits.
To consolidate a habit, what is known as the three R's of habits is required:
reminder, routine, and reward. The reminder is a stimulus that indicates we need to carry
out the behavior; the routine is the behavior itself, and the reward is the positive consequence
that comes from having carried it out. For example, it's Tuesday afternoon
and my calendar says 'exercise.' That is the reminder. Going for a run is the
behavior itself that I want to turn into a routine, and the reward will be one of the good things
that it provides me: feeling calmer, improving fitness, resting better, etc.
And why is it so hard for us to get rid of old habits? It's hard because, precisely,
the essence of habits is that they are carried out with almost no effort or conscious thought.
When we get distracted, there we are again behaving as we promised we wouldn't.
It takes a lot of effort to generate a positive habit as well as to lose a
negative one. Moreover, changing a bad habit for a more positive one is a very uneven competition:
we have to sacrifice an immediate short-term benefit for a more uncertain long-term one.
Deadline. And of course, that costs a lot. What is more rewarding in the short term, eating a
donut or a piece of fruit? Well, unless you come from a strange planet, the donut will
probably be more rewarding, even though you know that the fruit is better for your health. So,
to choose the fruit, you have to be very clear about your ideas and not succumb to the bad influence of the
environment. Because that's another difficulty: sometimes the environment leads us to maintain habits that do not
benefit us; the food industry invests billions to make us eat poorly;
daily stress makes it hard to find time to exercise; our friends
can pressure us to drink or smoke. A mistake we often make
when we want to change habits is being too ambitious; suddenly we 'see the light',
decide that things 'cannot go on like this' and, all of a sudden, we aim to eat better,
exercise three times a week, meditate, read, and quit social media. And sure,

on paper it may sound great. But the reality is that such abrupt changes are doomed to fail. It's very hard to suddenly give up the short-term benefits of those 'bad' habits, and it takes time to start seeing the fruits of the new ones.
Therefore, if you're considering a 'habit change', first try to create a
hierarchy: write down all the changes you want to make from most to least important in your life.
Review them, go over them, reorder them. And when you are clear about which is the most important or urgent for you,
start with that one. But don't try to do everything at once. Choose one, commit to that change,
make it easier to carry out, and make it hard to fail. For example: if you've chosen
to start with sports, set aside a fixed time during the week and don't even question whether to do it
or not. Just do it. And the more days you add, the more you'll reinforce the habit, until the moment
comes when it will be much easier for you. It won't be 'free' in terms of effort (only bad habits are
that, that easy) but it will be much less costly. Have you chosen to improve your diet? Review those foods you shouldn't be eating and start there. In fact,
as my friend Julio Basulto says, it's more important to stop eating poorly than to eat
well. Because the mistake we make is usually more about the excess of harmful foods
than a lack of other types of foods. Make that list (in fact, in his latest book
there's a pretty brief one to start with) and under no circumstances allow yourself those foods.
Do you have them at home? Throw them away. Don't buy them. And remember that the exception is what you do once
or twice a year, not once or twice a month. In summary, it is very hard to change habits
because of the very nature of habits that leads us to execute them automatically.
Don't try to change everything at once, but rather have a strategy, choose and commit to one
change at a time. That way, you will gain mastery over yourself and start to see progress that will
motivate you to incorporate more positive changes. And that's it for now, another dose of psychology,
